p:
Yes. We see it from two ends. A, from parents who come in for services, as you know. We see about 250 families a day who come through our door, and we look at them in holistic way, what do they need, benefits and also the ability to become self-sufficient and going to

work. And we also see that from the workforce development work that we do that we have parents who use– who are planning to enter the workforce, hoping that they’ll have a slot for their child, and they’re hearing that it might– that might not happen. So, we hear it from both ends. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Right. Well, thank you so much. Thank you for testifying. We’re hoping that we can figure out so much of what we heard today. I appreciate it.

Thank you. Good luck. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Yeah, of course. Thank you. Next, we’re going to move to our virtual panel. So, sorry. Did we miss anyone that is here present with us in chambers who wants to testify? Okay, wonderful. So, now we’re going to move to Zoom. Okay, first up is Elizabeth Ghunney.
You may begin.

Thank you. Good afternoon, Chair Gutiérrez. My name is Elizabeth Ghunney, Director of Home Base Child Care Services at the Women’s Housing and Economic Development Corporation, WHEDCO. Thank you for the opportunity to testify in support of the proposed Local Law

establishing an Office of Child Care and creating a path to free child care for all city residents within four years. WHEDCO strongly supports this law’s vision to make child care equitable and accessible for every family. It will be successful if it includes both informal and licensed family child care providers, promoting economic opportunity and a practical solution to increasing access in neighborhoods that need it most. For 30 years, WHEDCO has advanced this very vision. We support informal and licensed family child care providers as both early educators and small business owners. Home-based child care is essential infrastructure for working families. Providers offer trusted, flexible and culturally-responsive care in neighborhoods where community relationship matter deeply. They create developmentally-appropriate environments for infants and toddlers by offering small group sizes, individualized attention and consistent caregiving relationships that support early attachments, social/emotional development, and responsive learning. WHEDCO’s research and direct engagement with providers highlight several urgent needs that a dedicated Office of Child Care could address. First,

family child care businesses require consistent and accessible human resources support. Centralized HRA assistance could help families navigate employment regulations–
[interposing] Thank you for your testimony. Time has expired.

[inaudible] and professionalize their operations. Second, many home-based providers lack the capital needed to expand capacity, improve facilities, or adopt new educational resources. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Elizabeth, I’m sorry. Can you wrap up in the next 10 seconds?
Yes. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you.

WHEDCO stands ready to partner with the Council and this office to ensure that informal and licensed family child care providers are included meaningfully in the design and implementation of universal care. Thank you. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you so much. Next we have Amy Shea.
You may begin.

Good afternoon, Chair Gutiérrez and members of the subcommittee. My name is Amy Shea. ECE Program Manager for the Northeast region at the Low Income Investment Fund, or LIFT. LIFT is a leading national community development financial institution, CDFI, with the vision that everyone live in a community of equity, opportunity and wellbeing, and we deploy capital to ensure this reality. LIFT has invested in ECE facilities and ECE providers through capital grants, technical assistance and training, emergency disaster recovery, and policy advocacy and research. As a long-time partner to the city and to New Yorker’s community-based organizations, LIFT shares the Mayor and Council’s commitment to build an equitable city where families can access high-quality child care and housing that they can afford in the neighborhoods they call home. As the program manager for this region, I’ve worked with child care providers across the city, supporting them to make sure that facilities are safe, healthy, and climate resistant through our emergency facilities grants, that they’re able to operate stable businesses through our assessments and coaching and to access support to

care for children through our collaborative technical assistance hub, Family Child Care NYC. Personally, I’m thrilled about universal child care, as soon I will be seeking care for my own child. I fully intended to be there in person today, but my pelvic pain had other ideas. But at any rate, I really thank you fo the opportunity to share our thoughts and for the virtual option to join. LIFT recognizes that workers compensation and pay parity is critical to making universal child care a reality, and supports all efforts to increase wages for child care educators. But I will focus my comments on LIFF’s expertise in child care facilities and capital. First, we recommend that the city establish a child care facility’s fund to address much-needed investments in the physical infrastructure of child care. As the city expands access to 3K and monitors 2-Care, providers will require capital to ensure their facilities are healthy, safe, and conducive to learning. And LIFT’s–
[interposing] Thank you for your testimony. Time is expired.

[inaudible]

CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Amy, you can wrap up in the next 10 seconds, please.

Sure. Okay, so the first recommendation and then I have two more after that. So, first we recommend a child care facilities fund. Second, we urge the city to pay our capital our high-touch technical assistance, and building coaching so that providers can locate, negotiation, plan, finance, execute and sustain complex facilities projects to maintain strong operations. Third, like in Local Law Introduction 9, the city should address regulatory barriers to increase in the supply of child care, including zoning and fee structures and integrating child care to planning and community development. And finally, in agreement with Local Law Introduction 8, we recommend that the city examine public assets including affordable housing to understand where they could be converted to child care and to better serve across– CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: [interposing] Thank you.

across diverse neighborhoods of the city. So, LIFT stands ready to partner with

the city in the roll out of universal child care. And thank you so much for your time. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: THank you, Amy. Next we have Kate Hoy.
You may begin.

Hi there. Sorry about that. Having trouble with mute. Good afternoon, Chair Gutiérrez and members of the Subcommittee. My name is Kate Hoy. I’m Vice President of Children’s Services at the Inter Agency Council of Developmental Disabilities Agencies. IAC is a nonprofit membership organization serving the five boroughs of New York City and regions throughout New York State. We represent a diverse coalition of over 200 member agencies including nonprofit early intervention providers, 4410 Special Education preschool programs, family groups, and independent practitioners dedicated to supporting children and adults with intellectual developmental disabilities. We support the vision for universal child care. I’m here today with an urgent warning. True universal child care cannot be achieved if the path forward excludes children with developmental disabilities. As the city rightfully expands Early Childhood access, our

nonprofit intervention and 4410 providers are being pushed to the brink of collapse. In just the past month, two legacy early intervention providers, agencies that help build the system were forced to close their doors. Surviving programs are operating at deficits, kept alive only by private board grants. They do this because their mission is to serve these children, but good will is not a sustainable business model. Our reality is defined by wait lists, closed classrooms and a systemic brain drain, and we advance pay parity for the broader system that we, 4410 and EI tether to inadequate reimbursement rates. Our specialized educators are forced to leave the nonprofit programs they love for higher paying district jobs. Worse, our nonprofit programs are routinely forced to act as a zero interest bank for the city, which I know you heard about earlier, draining their reserves to float the city’s obligations for up to 10 months of the school year while battling shifting guidelines and crushing bureaucracy. Furthermore, the city is currently operating a one-way street when it comes to hiring. Former DOE staff are not permitted to work in our programs for up to two years. Yet, our staff are

frequently poached by the DOE. staff are often told they must accept an offered DOE position within a day or two, leaving our programs in a lurch and resulting in, again, publicly-placed public school children with disabilities with unfulfilled IEP mandates. Our programs are publicly funded and serve public students. Why are our providers paid so much less and provided– and expected to do so much more. We strongly support Intro 631 and ask that all reports and workforce initiatives explicitly include 4410 Early Intervention providers who need mandated salary parity and benefit parity. A system that is structurally disadvantaged disabled children isn’t universal, it’s exclusionary. We stand ready to partner with you to build a system that works for every child, and I will submit a much longer written testimony. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you. Thank you, Kate.
Thank you. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Next up we have Carolyn Cleveland.
You may begin.

Good afternoon, Chair Gutiérrez and members of the subcommittee. My name is Carolyn Cleveland and I’m Chief Operating Officer of the Kennedy Children’s Center. We are a 4410 community-based organization and IAC member that serves more than 400 preschoolers in Harlem and the Bronx and our students have some of the most significant developmental delays and disabilities in the public school system. While my written testimony focuses on three critical issues, I’m very grateful that two have already been highlighted extensively today. First, children with disabilities must be explicitly included in expansion planning and the city needs to partner, not compete, with early intervention and 4410 programs. Second, salary parity. We need to address unequal pay for Special Education staff at CBOs like mine. So, I’d like to focus on my last point for the speaking portion of the event which is staffing. As we all know, the Early Childhood field already has a severe staffing shortage and this is nothing new. In fact, after years of losing staff to the DOE and struggling to find and retain staff, the Kennedy Children’s Center actually created our own Grow Your Own Program from

scratch. Nearly 10 years later, we’ve trained more than 500 adults to become certified teacher assistants and we became a registered apprenticeship program with the Department of Labor in 2024, the first and only registered apprenticeship program in Early Childhood and Special Education. Today, we train about 100 certified teams annually, and we have 30 registered apprentices employed between our preschool, and more than 80 percent of our trainees and apprentices are women of color and most are working mothers. I am thrilled that the city sees the power and potential of apprenticeships and non-traditional teaching candidates, and I would welcome the opportunity to speak with more about our model. I want to thank you all for your attention to this very important topic. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you, Carolyn. The next panelist we have is Jenna Lautner [sp?]-- Lauter, sorry.
You may begin.

Thank you so much. My name is Jenna Lauter. I get Lautner all the time. And I’m a Policy Counsel at the New York Civil Liberties Union. Universal child care is a necessary

ingredient for thriving families and communities and a prerequisite for reproductive and gender justice. We are eager to see the city build towards a truly universal system in which every family is guaranteed access to child care regardless of income, geography, employment, disability, or immigration status. The NYCLU supports proposed investments in the Child Care Assistance program, 3K expansion, and thoughtfully implemented 2-Care. We also urge the City Council to continue to robustly fund the Promise NYC program to ensure that immigration status does not prevent families from accessing the child care that they need. We also join other advocate’s calls for urgent investment in the child care workforce. It is a gender and racial injustice that we continue to expect women of color, many of whom are parents themselves, to perform caregiving work for poverty wages, despite its importance of the backbone of our communities and economy. A thriving workforce is also essential to expanding child care capacity and access. We cannot achieve universal child care without ensuring that educators earn competitive wages. Critically, and what I really wish to add to this conversation, is that we urge the city to

disentangle child care administration from the family regulation system, including by eliminating any role for the Administration for Children's Services. ACS is fundamentally an investigatory and prosecutorial agency that separates thousands of children from their families each year. It disproportionately targets low-income communities of color, especially Black mothers, for surveillance and punishment most often based on their socioeconomic circumstances. Parents in these communities view ACS as a threat, a source of trauma and harm that they do not want involved in their lives. Even ACS Commissioner Dannhauser concedes that parents fear engaging in services provided by an agency with the power to take their children away. If we want families to fully take advantage of child care support, we cannot require them to seek it through or in connection with ACS. Thank you.
Thank you for your testimony. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you, Jenna. Next we have Ingrid Matias Chungata.
You may begin.

Good afternoon, Chair Gutiérrez. It’s a pleasure being here and to have you as a champion in Early Childhood and the subcommittee members of the Council. I’m Ingrid Matias Chungata, and I’m the Executive Director of Nuestros Ninos, a community-based organization in Williamsburg founded in 1973. We serve about 500 children across Brooklyn and Queens through center-based and family child care programs. And I want to say that I support universal child care. As a mother of four who left the workplace working in finance to take care of my children, because either I was working for child care or I would stay home and just raise my children. I was forced out of the workforce. And found the Early Childhood field to be that opportunity for me to work and take care of my children, so I founded a family child care program. So, with that said, the expansion of 2K recently and the additional seats, extended day 3K seats, is such an important progress in our city. But we cannot do this– and I think everyone who has spoken today have said– last that we stabilize the workforce and address one issue that we at Nuestros Ninos have been facing, and it’s getting our children the

developmental support that they need. So, organizations like Nuestros Ninos, have become the training grounds for DOE. We recruit educators. We mentor them. We support them through certification and provide them with flexibility as they complete their degrees. But once they get certified, they leave for higher paying job. And we cannot blame them. We work in– we live in a city that is super expensive. But without real pay parity between community-based programs and DOE universal child care we’ll continue to face staffing shortages and instability. Party parity is not an option. It’s foundational.
Thank you for your testimony. Time has expired. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Ingrid, you could wrap up. You need five more seconds?

I was just going to say that there’s three serious things that we need to look at. And it’s we need really to invest in the educators that are– are in our communities. We need to setup clear timelines for families to wait for evaluations that put children to wait for services and we also need to increase these resources to

eliminate these backlogs, something that Greg already mentioned which are the CBC clearance for our staff. Thank you. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you so much. Yes, of course. We have next up Rebecca Schneider-Kaplan. Rebecca Schneider-Kaplan?
You may begin. REBECCA SCHNEIDER-KAPLAN. Hi, good afternoon. Can you hear me? CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Yes, we can hear you.
I apologies. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: No worries.

thank you for allowing me to speak today. My name is Rebeca Schneider-Kaplan, Ms. Becky, and I’m a proud UPK 4 teacher at Stepping Stones Preschool in Staten Island. As the city looks forward to the future on their new journey of universal child care, I just want to say please don’t forget to look back and remember us, your community-based UPK staff. I support the plan for universal child care because every family deserves access to a free quality Early Childhood education. A positive start to a child's

education will help to determine future social/emotional and academic success. I wish there was universal child care in 2009, because I was a single mother with a toddler. I struggled to find full day child care as I completed student teaching. It took me two semesters to finish the required field work hours. I support the plan for universal child care, but I beg you to please stop and look in your rearview mirror first. You will see the dedicated men and women responsible for educating the majority of our’s EBK programs. We are waving our hands and begging not to be forgotten. Please don’t forget our assistant teachers. Please don’t forget our directors. They’ve gone seven years without contracts. Please don’t forget our students and please don’t forget our families and the implications it has had on us. I would like to suggest one idea to help resolve some of these issues, and that is for the New York Department of Education to hire all of your CBO staff members directly. We are not external employees. Our credentials are the same. Our curriculum is the same. We deserve the same contracts to the same union which is UFT, the same cost of living accommodations, and the same respect.

[inaudible] directly before you expand any further. I teach NYC because I want to make profound impact–
[interposing] Thank you for your testimony. Time has expired.
[inaudible]. I– CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: [interposing] You can wrap up, Rebecca in the next few seconds.
Sorry. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: No, no, thank you.
Please teach NYC that you will not turn your backs on us. Thank you. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you, Rebecca. Next we have Megan Elder.

Hi, good afternoon. Thank you for allowing me the opportunity to speak. My name is Megan Elder. I’m a UPK teacher also in Staten Island. I’ve been working the past few years after school as a seat [sic] provider and a sets [sic] provider. I’m speaking here today not only as an early educator and provider, but as a parent. I’m currently pregnant with my first child, and it has

been a real struggle working two jobs to make ends meet and to prepare for the arrival of my baby. It’s hard to– not to compare my situation to the teachers in public schools. We’re required to have the same degrees, the same certifications, the same work load and follow the same curriculum. I urge you to provide CBO workers the same benefits and salary as our DOE counterparts. For years, CBO schools have faced issues that have not been addressed by our city, including underpaid staff, no medical coverage, and lack of benefits, no cost of living adjustment for the last five years, and the expectation to have another two. Our directors here at my school, they’ve been supporting our UPK program out of their own pocket since the 90s. They make even less than us teachers. We’re responsible for the most important New Yorkers, our children. Every day we fuel the economy by giving parents the confidence to go to work without worries. They have peace of mind that their children are safe, loved, and learning in expert hands. However, we cannot keep working tirelessly for our city under these conditions. Thank you.

CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you, Megan, and congrats. All the best. Next up we have Adrienne Bond.
You may begin.
Hi, good afternoon. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Hello. I can hear you.
Hi, can you hear me? CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Yes.

Good afternoon, of course. My name is Adrienne Bond. I thank you for the opportunity to speak. I speak on behalf of Quick Start Day Care Center. We’re located in the Saint Albans, Queens, New York. I am not– I know a lot of what I’m saying may have been already stated, but I just want to testify firsthand on what happens when you don’t have pay parity, proper staffing, and money budgeting. Over the past two years, we are lucky and fortunate to hang in there and stay on, but we have gone quite a few months with no pay, and we’ve still managed to open up our doors and service as parents– working parents of the community. We struggled. We fought. We fought for two years in a row and we managed to stay alive, but it has been hard. We

begged for pay parity. We have lost a lot of our certified teachers to the DOE, because they don’t stay. They can’t stay if they’re not going to be able to afford the cost of living. The children start to leave if you don’t have proper staffing and that makes it a struggle. We just ask that they revisit everything all across the board, to take care of the directors, the education directors who work hard, the book keepers, the certified teachers, from the cooks to the janitors to everyone in the building. We just ask that they revisit it. Revisit the qualifications and skills that they ask of us to have that we do have to our counterparts located in the Department of Education. We’re no different. We fall under the same umbrella, servicing the children that show up Monday through Friday here to learn and we do our jobs with our hearts and soul. So, we just ask that they revisit this, because it is a trying time for everyone all across the board. And we want to remain open, and we would love to expand, but we need to be sure that the money is there, that they’re going to support the DOE, they’re going to support us and give us all the tools necessary to provide a

proper education that all the children deserve, what parents deserve–
[interposing] Thank you for your testimony. Time has expired.
[inaudible] I appreciate it. Thank you so much. Have a good day. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you, Adrienne. Our next panelist is D. Lashaun Brown.
You may begin. D.

Good afternoon. I would like to first thank the committee for welcoming all stakeholders and creating a space dedicated for this important work. I would first like to clarify that there’s a lot of talk about providing quality services. [inaudible] that has been community providing quality services for decades. So, I’d like to change that narrative and say continue to provide services to, again, respect to those who the system’s back was built on which is the community as well as churches and from grassroots advocacy. The sector has barely survived the first installment of universal child care under de Blasio, and these recent announcements wreak of the same challenges. It would stand to reason that fixing the current system

should be a priority for all across the city before anyone speaks about expansion. Many politicians have spoken about expansion in their district. However, we must consider the programs who are currently suffering. So, I pulled the following questions for consideration and thought. How do you propose to support expansion while programs within the same district are struggling and contracts do not allow for the flexibility of shifts and the types of age-based seats that are needed? How do you propose to support an expansion when you have a system that is competing with its funder for staff and children? I say this as I just received an email to teach for the DOE. How do you propose or support expansion when CBO programs must contend with the systemic bottlenecks that exist within DOE, DOH, DOB, FDNY, OMB, OLR, OCP, all of which directly or indirectly affect my m-o-n-e-y? How do you propose and support expansion for two-year-olds when the DOH contends that once a child turns three in a two-year room, you must have a teacher that qualifies at the same time that we are struggling with staffing. I am disappoint– well, how is there a voucher waiting list when you have centers who are not fully enrolled and

being impacted fiscally due to the way our contract is set up. I am disappointed that after all these years, those who have claimed to be diehard New Yorkers and–
[interposing] Thank you for your testimony. Time has expired. D.
Okay. Let me just wrap up. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: If you could just– yeah, yeah. Thank you. D.

Yes. This is not a one-person doom [sic]. This is a conundrum of bad actors, policies, and systems. I would like for the– while I don’t know the role of the City Council, I’m eager to see what actionable items come from them. Thank you. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you so much for your testimony. Happy to work together so that we can learn what the City Council is going to be able to do here. Next we have Alice Bufkin.
You may begin.

Good afternoon. My name is Alice Bufkin and I’m the Associate Executive Director of Data and Policy at Citizens Committee for

Children. Thank you, Chair Gutiérrez and Council Members, for this opportunity to testify. In 2023, CCC produced a report on barriers to child care access. We used administrative data, citywide surveys, interviews with parents and providers, and many of the key findings resonate as much today as they did then. Families face significant barriers to access, lack of knowledge of existing programs, and they find that the available options don’t match their needs and work schedules. So, we are really grateful that this administration and City Council are committed to tackling many of these challenges and we urge city leaders to continue using data on child and family needs to inform how the city delivers and expands its EC services. In the time I have today, I want to uplift a couple of key priorities. First, while we were very glad to see that funding for preschool special education was included in the Preliminary Budget, there are other areas of ECE funding that were not part of that budget. We urge the City Council to championing these priorities, including $5 million of continued funding for ECE outreach, as well as maintaining and increasing investments in Promise NYC. Second, we

remain deeply concerned about the city’s ability to eliminate the child care voucher wait list. While we were reassured by the Governor’s investments, we know this funding is inadequate, as we heard about frequently today, to address the voucher crisis in New York City which has left approximately 16,000 families on wait lists. We urge the mayor and City Council to continue working with the state to meet the need and prepare to address shortfalls with city funding. Third, we echo what so many have emphasized today, and the ECE system that is built on the deeply inadequate and inequitable pay of our community-based child care workforce will not be sustainable. The challenges of pay equity and compensation structures are even greater for preschool special educators and for family child care providers. It’s urgent that the city thoughtfully incorporate family child care providers into 2K implementation and address the structural and pay inequities that have forced so many providers to close. What we need now is not just acknowledgement from the administration of the need for parity, we need a concrete plan to achieve it. And finally, we believe it is critical to

approach a path to universal child care with a focus on those most marginalized by the existing system.
Thank you for your testimony. Time has expired.
[inaudible] families and students [inaudible] CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: You can wrap up.
Thank you. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you so much, Alice. Next we have Shanita Bowen.
You may begin.

Thank you, Chair Gutiérrez, for allowing us to testify today. My name is Shanita Bowen, Chief Operating Officer for ECE On the Move. would have loved to have been there in-person. ECE On the Move is a grassroots organization with the voices of over 700 family child care providers and their families that they’re serving. And we have to say that we agree with the Rabbi’s earlier testimony about the wait list. But first, I want to say that families are placed on a wait list. This is something we’ve experienced before historically, and parents used to go there where their case was never resurrected. And so

parents are cutting off their work hours, turning down opportunities, rearranging their lives just to survive. This waiting list is hurting all of our lives. At this moment, parents and educators only have each other. With family child care educators stretching themselves to hold children, hold spots, hold families together while everyone waits for help. Well, where are the systems that are supposed to help educators. Where is the leadership helping both families and educator’s lives stabilize the families– I’m sorry, their financial lives. We show up for families every day, and who is showing up for us. And while we are showing up, we are doing it without stability ourselves. Family child care educators are caregivers, business owners, employers for mandating staffing. We are the wraparound support for entire communities, yet we cannot offer our own assistance. You asked the question earlier what is stopping the workforce from growing. What’s stopping the workforce from growing is that no one wants to enter being an educator when the pay is at minimum wage or slightly above without benefits. And we’re talking about family child care and utilizing us in a Pre-K system, the new 2-K, right?
Thank you for your testimony. Time has expired.

We have to fund the workforce fully, get rid of the wait list. People are there now. Eradicate them, and then move on to new systems, please. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you. Thank you so much Shanita. And our next panelist is Christopher Leon Johnson.
You may begin.

Yeah. Hello. My name is Christopher Leon Johnson. I want to make this clear that, look, the current plan for universal child care, I think that it’s a slow rigged process just to line up these nonprofits and union’s pockets. The city has enough money to do universal child care. The way that Mamdani pandered to the Governor to only roll out a crappy phase of the universal child care in the state for the city is really abysmal. This is nothing but a grift by the nonprofits just to line their pockets. If they– they could easy– and the City Council could easy get the– have the budget for universal child care, but the thing is that this is– this is nonprofit industrial complex in a nutshell.

Like, we’re for child care. Me and you are for child care but [inaudible] who was nothing but the attack dog for Justin Brannan. I’m surprised he still didn’t get a job in the Mayor’s Office yet. But this is– this is bullcrap. I mean, this is like– I think the people need to start calling stuff out, and start calling out these organizations like for child care fraud for prolonging stuff. This is nothing but the NPIC [sic] in a nutshell. Straight up NPIC crap in a nutshell when it goes to child care. Just like how tomorrow when Transportation Alternatives is going to keep prolonging the process with street [inaudible]. But basically, look, this could be solved today. This could be solved in this current budget. This city, all they got to do is start cutting out some of these non– basically the home-based nonprofits, their money, and then you have enough money to give child care every year for the next four, eight years, under the Mamdani administration until the next mayor comes. But this is my advice is that you got to readjust the budget. You got to start cutting these things, the homeless industrial complex nonprofits, like WIN and all these non– that just take all our

money and does nothing with it. And I mean, that’s a start. I mean, take all their money–
[interposing] Thank you for your testimony. Time has expired.

for the child care nonprofits. So, taking child care– thank you so much. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you, Christopher. Excellent. And now, with that, I believe that is our last panelist to testify on Zoom. Okay, great. I want to thank everybody who stayed, everyone who is virtual. I want to thank, of course, the Office of Child Care Executive Director Emmy Liss for staying the whole time, DC Hawkins from DOE was also here for a significant amount of time. Thank you everybody for the robust testimonies, conversations to our Speaker who was here in the beginning. I look forward to the next hearing, and I think– I want to thank my staff, too. Thank you all so much. That adjourns today’s hearing. [gavel]

Quiet down, please. Good morning, and welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Technology. Good morning, and welcome to our first hearing. I'm Council Member Carmen De La Rosa, Chair of the Committee on Technology. Thank you for joining us for today's oversight hearing on facial recognition technology and the collection of biometric data. We will hear two bills, Proposed Intro. 213-A sponsored by Council Member Hanif in relation to prohibiting places or providers of public accommodations from using biometric recognition technology and protecting any biometric identifier information collected and Intro. 428 sponsored by Council Member Pierina Sanchez in relation to limiting the use of facial recognition technology in residential buildings.

This is my first hearing as a Chair of the Committee on Technology, and I'm very excited to start this session with this important topic. Facial recognition technology was introduced years ago and, since then, it has advanced rapidly in both accuracy and accessibility. It is without question an impressive and innovative tool. Today, it allows individuals to unlock their phones instantly, secure access to devices and sensitive files, and enhance certain security systems. Used responsibly and with appropriate safeguards, facial recognition technology offers convenience and efficiency. However, like many powerful technologies, its impact depends entirely on who is using it and how it is used. Some argue that facial recognition is necessary for public safety. Cameras are now present on many street corners, in public accommodations, transportation systems, retail stores, and even residential buildings. Yet the widespread presence of cameras and facial recognition systems has not by itself eliminated crime. Retailers may argue that facial recognition helps combat shoplifting and organized retail theft. However, long-term theft statistics in New York City from 2006 to 2024 show that overall trends have generally

increased, with temporary declines during the 2020 lockdown and slight decreases in 2023. Technology alone has not proven to be the comprehensive solution. Additionally, no technology is perfect. Facial recognition systems still misidentify individuals. According to testing by the National Institute of Standards and Technology, error rates can be below one percent when analyzing high-quality controlled images such as mug shots. However, when images are less clear, such as those captured by surveillance cameras in real-world conditions, the error rate can increase significantly, in some cases approaching 20 percent. Even if accuracy could be perfectly improved, serious concerns still remain. What happens when a person is wrongfully flagged as a criminal because he or she is standing near someone else, resembles another individual, or were mistakenly included in a database? What recourse does that person have to correct inaccurate information? Is there a transparent process for review and removal? Consider another scenario. A person who once committed a minor offense out of necessity or under duress or by accident, should that individual be

permanently barred from entering grocery stores or denied housing because of biometric data stored in a private system? Without clear standards and due process protections, private entities may impose penalties without transparency or an opportunity for appeal. We have already seen this technology used beyond traditional security context. Madison Square Garden made headlines for using facial recognition technology to deny entry to certain attorneys involved in litigation against the company. That raises an important question. Where are the boundaries? Could this technology be used to exclude individuals based on profession? Could it be misused to discriminate based on political views, skin tones, backgrounds, or other characteristics? The risks become even more significant when facial recognition is combined with artificial intelligence and other data sets. Could facial recognition data be linked to financial records, credit scores, tax information, purchasing history, or family status? Could individuals be excluded based on income level? Could different services be provided based on data that has been aggregated about a cost a customer? These concerns are no longer theoretical.

And one more thing, unlike a password or a credit card, a face cannot be easily changed. Once biometric data is captured, the risk could be permanent. Unfortunately, the law often lags behind technological advances. This is why thoughtful action is necessary now. Innovation should not come at the expense of fundamental rights. Clear guardrails are essential. Transparency is how systems operate meaningful consent, limits on data retention and sharing, strong anti-discrimination protections, independent oversight, and accessible mechanisms to correct errors. Facial recognition technology is not inherently good or bad. It is a powerful tool. But its impact depends not only on how it's designed, but also on how it is used and for what purpose. Because of its power, it demands careful governance and clear boundaries. Our responsibility is to ensure that as technology evolves, it does so in a way that protects privacy, prevents discrimination, safeguards due process, and maintains public trust. The goal is not to slow innovation. The goal is to ensure that innovation serves people without compromising their rights.
